newsitem.title: USA: NY Gov says still issues open in NYC tax extension.
newsitem.headline: NY Gov says still issues open in NYC tax extension.

text.p: New York State Gov. George Pataki on Tuesday told reporters in Albany that issues remained to be settled in talks with New York City officials over extending a city tax surcharge but added the two sides were not far apart.

"We're close, there's a chance, and there are a couple of outstanding issues," Pataki said, explaining those issues were the size of the city's police force and how long New York City's personal income tax surcharge would be extended.

The 12.5 percent surcharge, which has helped pay for 6,000 new police officers for the city, is projected to raise $455 million in the city's 1997 fiscal year, but it expires at year-end unless the state legislature extends it.
Pataki indicated that his fellow Republican, Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, appeared to have opened the window to some compromises over how the funds would be spent.

"I don't believe that he (Giuliani) has changed his position, he is willing to go along with less flexibility than he otherwise would have had under some of the earlier negotiated bills we were talking about," he said.

The New York Times in its Tuesday edition said that the tax extension talks between Giuliani, who wanted more freedom to spend the money as he determined, and the state's top Democrat, Sheldon Silver (D-Manhattan), who wanted written assurances from Giuliani that he would use a substantial share of the money to hire more police officers, had broken down.

But Pataki tempered his optimism over whether the state legislature, which he called into special session on Tuesday, would reach agreement on the personal income tax surcharge and on another bill the city seeks, one that would create a new infrastructure authority to sidestep its debt cap.
"On both the personal income tax and the infrastructure authority I think we're a long way along, but we're not entirely there yet," he said.
Pataki appeared most positive over a plan to reform how New York City's schools are governed, another of the key issues that the special session, which might be as short as one day, will address.

"We are very, very close, and I am extremely optimistic that we will soon be passing historic legislation that will finally add real accountablity in the schools of New York City and the kids and the parents are going to be the winners."

The governor said Giuliani had agreed that the bill should provide for a statement detailing how much aid for New York City's schools is contributed by the city, the state, sand the federal government.
